entry.title: Unsaid Things Lately
entry.content:
“Is it better to speak, or to die?”

I ask myself that question more often than not. Lately, that phrase has become more relevant, as I currently battle unsaid thoughts and feelings for that matter.

Lately, I’ve been wanting to be with my only close friends, for whom I can tell about everything. Last Friday, that longing was so intense, that I thought about shifting a course, just to be with one of them. I never really had many friends for whom I can rant my problems to, and it makes me sad because a good friend is all I need to speak to.

I was feeling a mixture of feelings as of late. I feel like I’m lost, I feel like I’ve been disappointing myself, I feel like I want a new start, I feel like I want to just speak the unspeakable. All of these feelings never reached the ear or the eye of a person. Only my journal writings saw the struggle to even describe those feelings. Honestly, I just want to be loved, not by my family or friends, but by someone. That’s actually one of the feelings I’ve felt as of late.

I thought, I would experience the start of something, when I somehow met (online) someone in a forum. We exchanged Instagrams and talked for several days, but it ended when that person stopped responding. We were supposed to meet so I can tour that person in a place. But that person just disappeared. Then, I grew a feeling, an early-stage feeling for someone in my school. I don’t even know why because it felt so random. I never saw that person’s face for more than 5 minutes, but the glimpse was enough to attract me. It’s so weird and shallow to be honest, but who am I to say that what I’m feeling is not true?

Is it just a coping mechanism or reaction because of the stress and uncertainty I’ve been feeling since the school started? I don’t know. I want to know.

So answer the question. Is it better to speak, or to die?

My answer would be to die, but I want, so badly to speak. But I’m so afraid. I want to speak to someone who could convince me that dying is not the option. I want a person, or a set of people, to listen when I do have the courage to speak. I want all of these but I don’t have them right now.

(Disclaimer: The word ‘dying’ is used metaphorically here, as the original phrase meant.)
entry.summary: “Is it better to speak, or to die?”

entry.title: Remain A Little Prince
entry.content:
Being a kid felt so easy, or perhaps, it’s better to say eager. We used to be so eager to play, we were so excited to go outside and enjoy the day ahead.

That feeling as a kid is naturally lost as we grow up, and personally, I feel like I’m at the crossroads between being a kid and an adult. I will be turning 20 in less than 100 days, that fact doesn’t really make me happy or excited as I think about it now. As a kid, I wanted to be an adult fast so I can have money and be “free”, but as my time for adulthood is nearing, I just want to remain a kid forever, like the Little Prince.

I was fortunate enough not to be told what to do. I was free to choose my course and most of my decisions in life. But there is still that push factor making me choose something that will be practical. I could be doing other, more fun things today, but I don’t have the privilege to do so.

I was just scrolling on my gallery from 2-3 years ago… I see a person who does not care about the future value of what he’s doing, but a person who does what he loves. I can’t say the same today as even if I do actually love what I do, the fact that I’m doing it for the future rather than my enjoyment makes it not the same. School really breaks any serious love I have for what I’m doing, I feel like a robot just attending lectures and doing course works just to pass.

I hope I remain a little Prince who cares for one thing- his rose, or the thing that he loves. I hope I don’t become Mr. Prince who just follows what society demands.

That’s it for today. Maybe I’m just tired.

(I just watched the movie a few days ago because of Lev Lazarev’s Free Program theme. I honestly haven’t read the book yet, I am supposed to read it back in 10th grade, but my interest in literature was close to none back then that I probably AI’d my way through the required reflections, which I absolutely regret and feel ashamed now.)
entry.summary: Being a kid felt so easy, or perhaps, it’s better to say eager. We used to be so eager to play, we were so excited to go outside and enjoy the day ahead.

entry.title: Am I the same boy?
entry.content:
I vaguely remember a poem we used to recite every some afternoon when I was in 6th grade, I remember a fragment of it saying—Am I the same girl? I used to delight… the cookies and ice cream, the pastries mother baked. That poem, by an unknown author, still has me questioning myself from time to time—Am I the same boy? Or have I stayed the same, still the kid I once was.

People change, all the time—so was I. I hold a strong opinion that the majority of my childhood changed compared to now. But I still like the idea that some things never changed.

I’ve grown to be the same kid, who just get good grades. From Elementary until Senior High School, and I hope until College. Good grades to me have always meant having an Honor, having a 90+ GWA became my standard of good enough, that getting a line of 8 means a failure to me. I don’t like to call myself smart, but if having Honors means that, then I am smart since 1st grade. But since my idea of being smart changed some time in High School, I saw grades as just a number you get for getting good scores. Good scores that, most of the time, just requires you to memorize facts. But I am not a genius, my grades in math haven’t always been up to my standards and my voice still shakes when I am talking to people—I hope this changes.

I’ve grown to believe what I now believe. Let’s talk about religion, when you are born in a predominantly Catholic country, you are bound to become one. As a great writer wrote before I was even born—”There is no such thing as a Christian child: only a child of Christian parents.” So when I was born, I was baptized, and the rest is history. If you already know what I’m going to confess, great. But I am… not religious—I am an agnostic atheist since 2021. This belief of mine towards religion is just a personal realization of the conflicting ideas religion has and my own views of the world. I still celebrate Christmas out of respect, I still go to church when my family and friends invite me to, I still pray to someone when I am vulnerable. Yet, I am an atheist—I hope people understand that I mean no harm towards their own religious views, and I believe we should be free to believe whatever brings us peace.

I’ve grown to be more comfortable feeling what I feel. Here is another confession, I am not straight. I’ve always had a feeling back then that I may be gay or “bakla,” as they call us, yet because of societal expectations, I just shrugged it off and forced myself to conform to what is allowed—that a man should only fall in love with a woman, and vice versa. This idea, that I do like both, is still queer to me. To be honest, I am not fond of calling myself a specific spectrum of the LGBT+ because what I know I feel is simple. I am attracted to men physically, but I am still open to having the expected relationship with my opposite. I am a male, call me he and him, that will never change—And I don’t want to complicate things further because I am comfortable expressing how I feel this way, but again, respect should be given to those who might feel otherwise.

I’ve also grown to see myself change stances in social, ethical, and philosophical matters. As I grew older, and got more aware, it should be given that my views change and grow as well. The facts we think are true may well change in the future. Also, I find people to be a joke sometimes. I find it funny how people can claim like they know it, and claim that a thing is good or bad, so they leave no room for others to question their opinions. I think people lack the openness to be wrong—and this is the easiest way to be a fool.

Change will always happen. In nature, in society, in ourselves. So to answer the question: Am I the same boy?

The answer is no, but I am still here. So I am free to believe that some things never change.

Or have I stayed the same, still the kid I once was.

entry.title: How to manage all your interests

link.title: How to manage all your interests

entry.content:
(Note from 13-Sep-2026: I don’t know where I found this list, or if I wrote it somehow. I must have copied it from a website somewhere or from a YouTube video I watched.

I think this list is really cool and fits the nature of this blog.)

Make a Graveyard

  • A list of thoughts that comes into mind, it could be a cool project, a want to buy, or anything that you want to do, but can’t at the moment.

Look for Life Multipliers

  • Skills or activities that have an implication in other areas of life that will give you the most benefit.

Make Your “Must-Do” List

  • Similar to the idea of “Bucket List” where you write anything that you want to achieve or do in your lifetime. The items in the list may not last long, because interests come and go, but having a list gives you a road map or an overview on what your life goals are.

Do a Time Audit

  • Auditing how much we spend on something can help us know how much time we need to do something, and it also helps us realize when we are wasting our time. For instance, knowing that we are spending hours watching TikTok can be a wake up call to us. Just like in finances, a time well audited can present a lot of opportunities for optimization and avoiding wasted resources, that is our time.

Change Your S.U.P. (smallest unit of productive time)

  • The SUP, or the smallest unit of productive time is a realistic time frame where you can have progress in a certain area of life or interest. For instance, an SUP for being mindful through meditation could be a 10 minute uninterrupted time where you really get to focus without any distractions. The SUP should be realistic and flexible because the days are not equal in a sense that one day could be a super productive day because you had a good sleep, while there could be lazy days where that SUP is not enough to even get focused.

Avoid Zero Days

  • Consistency is key. Do a little bit everyday because it builds a habit, even if the progress is small and marginal. Having zero days means you show up no matter what.

entry.title: I cannot get Young Hearts (2024) out of my head

link.title: I cannot get Young Hearts (2024) out of my head

entry.content:
I watched Young Hearts yesterday because I finally searched it up after seeing the opening up/car scene on Instagram. Now that I’ve watched it, I cannot seem to get it out of my head. I don’t know if it is because of the beautiful and wonderful actors that played the main roles, or because I can’t move on from the movie’s idealistic story. Just for the record, I watched Close (2022) today, and damn, it was the complete opposite. But we are talking about Young Hearts here.

When the movie started, I was immediately drawn to Elias, he is a fine man but is still very much a kid. What will unravel as the movie progresses is the early age in which the two lead characters fell in love and also accepted themselves being in love with the same gender. They are only 14 years old in the film, and when I try to remember what I felt when I was 14, I just remember myself liking boys but is still pretty much hiding my identity, which is still the case now. When Alexander told Elias about his first experience of falling in love, I was shocked when he said it was a boy. Elias did not say anything to hopefully know his ideas of such things at an early age, but Alexander seems to have accepted already. Alexander never mentioned the word “gay or bi” to describe himself until one scene later in the film where Elias contrasted himself as not being Alexander which he called “gay”. Even the friends of both Elias and Alexander seem to have this idea already about homosexual love. It seems like Elias is the only one who does not know or accept it yet.

I think the turning point of their relationship was the barn scene, where they were caught up by rain and went to the barn for a roof. That scene itself screams the intimacy of young love. Elias has been looking at Alexander throughout the film, looking at him in a very close and intimate way already, but this scene cemented that looking into love. Alexander just kissed Elias as they looked very close at each other. This is another proof for me that Alexander is way ahead of his age for things like this.

But here comes man vs society but more like man vs self. Elias, still not saying anything about his love for Alexander, felt the need to now show it when people are around. When Alexander hugged Elias in front of their schoolmates and Elias turned him away, it was a turning point for them but more for Elias because we can see again how Alexander has accepted himself, while Elias still needs to accept himself too. When Alexander and Elias talked about it, we can see Alexander asking if Elias really likes him or not and Elias finally saying yes. But this yes is still coupled with some sort of anxiety about how society will react about their relationship. Again, Alexander does not care about this while Elias still does. This scene is the climax for me, as it made Elias journey into self-acceptance.

Elias, while obviously having a feeling for Alexander, is still with his girlfriend. She later discovered Elias and Alexander’s affection when she saw them sort of hugging. She just knew upon seeing them that close. You gotta feel bad at least for the girl, but you cannot also blame Elias for not revealing his feelings for Alexander as he himself seems not to know the answer yet. Previously, there was a scene of Elias and his girlfriend being together and sleeping together, and Elias waking up, and rushing to Alexander’s house. Maybe this is the point where Elias knew that he was more in love with Alexander. But this scene is one that is hard to watch too. Elias attempted to kiss Alexander, but Alexander did not let him. I don’t know what message this scene is supposed to make. I’m conflicted whether this is Alexander keeping his distance as he felt distanced when Elias pushed him away, or it is some sort of sign that when Elias finally knows he loves him that he also lost that love for him.

The succeeding minutes will make you feel sad, and also worried. I was worried that I would be heartbroken as well by the end of the movie. I thought that it would all go down from this point on. But I’m wrong. This movie has an environment that is so ideal, that the only problem was Elias not accepting himself.

Their fight did not end with that. When Elias and Alexander are both at a party with their friends. We will witness them drifting from each other. At first, Elias just kissed his girlfriend (which is still a bit questionable since it is unclear whether they broke up or not). Alexander knew this, but they just went on to the party until it went south. Elias broke out of anger or denial when Alexander did a dare to kiss another boy. To be honest, what happened next really tainted Elias a bit. When they kissed, emotions flooded Elias and stormed out. Their friends followed him, along with Alexander. Elias broke out, saying things like “I am not like him [Alexander], I am not gay.” The exact words are better known when you watch this movie. But what Elias said definitely tainted their relationship as Alexander heard all of it. Alexander pushed Elias and cursed him. (I left a very important point where Elias and Alexander journeyed together because it is also better known when you watch the movie, but I also felt that it just showed a glimpse of what Alexander’s environment is that made him accept himself.)

I really thought it would have a bad ending.

After that fight, Elias went to isolation. He did not go home nor in school but instead went to his grandfather. They went on a trip together, wherein we saw Elias finally confess about his love for Alexander, although he said it without much words. His grandfather accepted him wholeheartedly, which adds to the idealism of this movie. That kind of acceptance from others is very much not the case in many countries and families, yet Elias just got accepted for the first time without any negative reactions. Then, we arrive at the car scene, where Elias opened up to his mother. Like the grandfather, this scene showed his mother totally accepting him. In this scene, we finally hear from Elias himself, that he is in love with Alexander. Previously we just assumed based on their closeness, but we finally hear a word: Elias loves Alexander.

Now, the ending. Elias now accepts himself, his family accepting him as well (the dad did later but still the same wholehearted and idealistic acceptance), he is finally ready to show that he is indeed in love with Alexander. We can see him in the end, hanging out with his friends, including his still unclear whether they broke up girlfriend. But when Elias saw Alexander, he sprinted out and got hit. His girlfriend went to him, Elias saying he saw Alexander, and we see his (I will now end them myself) ex-girlfriend freeing him in a way. His brother did the same next, so Elias was ready to see Alexander since they fought. Finally, they saw each other among the crowd.

Elias went to Alexander, Alexander smiled, then Elias kissed him. Alexander’s father is shown to be so happy (which once again shows this wholehearted acceptance), we can also see Elias’ mother smiling, and finally Elias’ father sees his son kissing another man. I thought his father would be the one to break the mood, but he completed it. The whole family accepted them both. And we saw them finally being happy together at that moment. The movie ended with a joyful play between the friend group of Elias and Alexander, with the two of them riding a bike. Alexander is pedaling while Elias is in the back, hugging him. What a beautiful and idealistic movie indeed. It is a movie that saw a character accept what he felt, without too much backlash.

entry.title: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.

link.title: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.

entry.content:
How this quote captures my ultimate goals in life

To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield. —”Ulysses” by Alfred Lord Tennyson

This line, from a poem “Ulysses” by Alfred Lord Tennyson, is one of my favorite quotations that lives rent free in my mind. It is a quote so powerful, that I consider it my life motto, and a quote I would likely want to engrave on my tombstone. It is not even a complete sentence, yet it captures the very idea of what a whole life should be.

We like a quote for many reasons; it sounds cool, it reflects an idea we like or our own personality, or it makes us better persons. The latter is the reason for me liking this quote.

When I think about this quote, I think of my ultimate goals in life:

  • I want to improve myself through constant learning. I don’t want to die knowing that I settled. I don’t want myself to be that person who stops growing after college.
  • I want to experience a lot of things. I don’t want to live my life doing what is the default (study>work>have a family>work>retire). I don’t want to die a slave, not having experienced the wonders of the world and my dreams.
  • I want to find out, fail, and succeed. I want to explore what I want to do in life, I want to experience failure which will help me grow, and I want to succeed because I persevered.
  • I want to be me. I want to live my life how I want it, to not let other people dictate my life’s direction. I want to be proud of myself because it was me who dreamed, worked, and succeeded in my goals.

This quote perfectly advocates for a life of constant improvement and exploration. It advocates for finding our inner sense of identity and purpose. And it inspires us not to give up.
entry.summary: How this quote captures my ultimate goals in life

entry.title: Why I write literature and media notes

link.title: Why I write literature and media notes

entry.content:
Staring at a blank page makes me want to be the best writer that ever lived. Although the great writers often died long before their written thoughts became known, I’d like to think that most of them never intended their writing to be seen in the first place. Now, writing literature (written) notes feels like a meta-practice, it is essentially writing about someone else’s writings. Similarly, writing media (non-written) notes is just writing about the creative creations of others, be it in the form of a movie, a show, or others. But why separate “literature” and “media”? The reason for that is simple: the media is the message. A book will convey a different message than a limited-by-runtime movie, but anyways, it doesn’t really matter.

The following reasons for writing these notes are listed below in no particular order:

Second Brain

Having a so called “second brain” is just a fancy way of saying this: My brain will forget, but I don’t want to forget, thus I need a way for my thoughts to be preserved indefinitely.

Any system of preserving our thoughts other than remembering them will serve the purpose of mitigating our lack of an indefinite memory. In the past, this was done by carving messages into stones or printing on paper. But in our digital age, it has never been easier to store an abundant amount of information conveniently. Digital data doesn’t forget or just disappear by design, but technology still fails, so the information we store on digital mediums is still indefinite. But it is better than our own memory.

Meditating on different ideas

Ideas come and go, and with the advent of technology, it has never been easier to flood our minds with information, it can be useless information or a useful one, but nonetheless both will just come and go. If we don’t take the time to think and meditate about them, then we are just consuming.

What I’m trying to do by writing these notes is to have a reason to meditate upon useful ideas that I come across. It should hold me accountable by forcing my lazy brain to slow down and digest what I’m learning from my daily consumption of information. Consuming content is the same as amusing ourselves to death (Postman reference). I’ve consumed enough in my lifetime, but I meditated very little. I don’t want to die one day and regret not taking the time to think, and be creative.

Being creative

There is creativity within us, we just have to find a medium and a reason to unleash it. Not everyone will consider themselves as a creative person, but how sad will life be without a little creative space? I personally feel a deep creative passion inside me, and I believe everyone has it deep inside them as well.

To unleash this deep creative desire of mine, I’ve tried many ways of creating and sharing it. I have written pages upon pages of journals, wrote essays when I feel like “being creative,” and also tried some ways of sharing it, but it never got consistent. Writing and sharing my notes or essays on various things I consume is one way to be creative consistently. I will never stop consuming, so I want to never stop being creative as well.

Sharing my thoughts

Lastly, what is the purpose of being creative when I’m the only one who can enjoy my work? While the motivation and purpose for taking notes is largely for my personal fulfillment, it does not hurt to share my thoughts. Publishing my notes allows me to share what I learn, and think to others. I don’t claim my insights to be largely important, I don’t share because I think I am influential in any sense. But to those who will stumble upon my writings, and will find them useful for their own lives, it is my pleasure to have you read my ramblings.

So welcome to this blog, where I share my notes on various literature (books, articles, and others…) and media (movies, shows, and others).

entry.title: A journey from indoctrination to liberation (Educated by Tara Westover)

link.title: A journey from indoctrination to liberation (Educated by Tara Westover)

entry.content:
“The past is beautiful because one never realises an emotion at the time. It expands later, & thus we don’t have complete emotions about the present, only about the past.” —VIRGINIA WOOLF

“I had been educated in the rhythms of the mountain, rhythms in which change was never fundamental, only cyclical. The same sun appeared each morning, swept over the valley and dropped behind the peak. The snows that fell in winter always melted in the spring. Our lives were a cycle—the cycle of the day, the cycle of the seasons—circles of perpetual change that, when complete, meant nothing had changed at all. I believed my family was a part of this immortal pattern, that we were, in some sense, eternal. But eternity belonged only to the mountain.” —TARA WESTOVER

What if I’m born into a different family? What if I’m born into a different country or century? Would I be the same person?

I asked these questions every time I tried to imagine myself in Tara’s life. I was never born into an ultra-religious family, nor was I born into one which thinks of the worst possible scenarios all the time. I wasn’t born into a time where I cannot go to the medical establishments when I get sick, nor was I born to be indoctrinated rather than educated. I was born into a family, a place and time which I now take for granted.

Unlike me, Tara was born into a family whose beliefs left a deep mark on her life. This mark was destructive, fatalistic, and undeserved. Tara lived a life of danger, made more dangerous by the fact that they did not seek medical help when they truly needed it. Tara was raised to believe that the government is against them, that the medical establishments are there to hurt them—set by the government, and that everyone who isn’t like them are evil-socialist-whore. Tara was not given the opportunity to be educated normally throughout her childhood and adolescence, where she goes to school with people of similar ages because her father believed that schools are brainwashing institution set up by the government. She was born into this world.

But like me, we shared some similarities, or I thought similar enough to feel like we had the same experiences. Those similar experiences echoed throughout the book.

The dangers of false beliefs, either by faith or by fear

I could not help myself but assume that the turning point where Tara’s father became the way he is, fearful and anxious, was when the Ruby Ridge incident happened. The book opened this topic quickly in the beginning and I cannot stop attributing it to his father’s behavior, this is considering how Tara described her father as being a completely different father to his older brothers.

“The older boys—Tony, Shawn and Tyler—had been raised in a different decade, and it was almost as if they’d had different parents. Their father had never heard of the Weavers

That history did something to their father.”

As a result, the rest of their siblings, including Tara, were raised in isolation, no official birth certificates, no attending school, just them at Buck’s Peak. Their father believed that the government is going to target them next, this fear did something to their father. This is a kind of false belief induced by fear.

The other dangerous kind of belief is induced by faith. This kind of faith in something: a God or an idea of something can be seen throughout the book.

Their father believed so much in their faith that he is willingly risking the lives of his children just because he had a false belief against the medical establishments. He thinks that God will cure everything, or he thinks that God has a deterministic plan for their family.

There were many instances in the book where faith won against reason. There were so many things that could have ended badly, or someone could have died. And for what?

A child indoctrinated is a child deprived of freedom

What kind of liberty is lost from indoctrination?

Freedom to think for ourselves, this is what Tara did not have the freedom to do, not until entering college.

The book can be summed up to this phrase: A journey from indoctrination to liberation.

Life in isolation brings a fascinating view into what it means to live a good life

(unfinished)

Truth and change reveals itself slowly, one realization, one shift at a time

(unfinished)

The importance of being educated

(unfinished)

The book ended in a powerful note:

“You could call this selfhood many things. Transformation. Metamorphosis. Falsity. Betrayal.

I call it an education.”
entry.summary: “The past is beautiful because one never realises an emotion at the time. It expands later, & thus we don’t have complete emotions about the present, only about the past.” —VIRGINIA WOOLF

entry.title: Would you feel sympathy for a killer? (Adolescence 2025)

link.title: Would you feel sympathy for a killer? (Adolescence 2025)

entry.content:
Here’s a dilemma: An innocent looking, 13-year-old boy, was accused of killing a girl similar to his age. There was concrete video evidence, but there’s a missing piece—more than the weapon, but the Why?

Motives for crimes are a secondary intel behind the actual evidence—the whys don’t justify the fact. The motive has little or no impact on the verdict to a crime as killing for a reason is not that different to another reason, not unless it is for “self defense” or war, or any other ways we as a society legalized killing another person.

Beyond the dilemma of why, we as the audience, can fall into the trap of the show. They made the accused killer seem innocent, besides, he was just a child—he’s not that scary. We can fall into the trap of attaching hope that this boy will be proven innocent and freed. The show created a facade which can make us sympathize with the accused killer, and I don’t think it’s unreasonable to feel that sympathy especially when watching the first 2 episodes only. The boy pleads he did not do it, and you can see a glimpse in his eyes and tone of voice that he didn’t.

The Season 1 of the show has a limited run of 4 episodes. Episode 1 followed the arrest and initial questioning of the accused. Episode 2 followed the police trying to find answers on the victim and accused killer’s school. Episode 3 followed a psychologist interviewing the boy. And Episode 4 follows the boy’s family months after the chaos.

Episode 1: The chaos

The police raided the Miller family’s house like a terrorist was inside. No showing of search or arrest warrant, just pure force, just to arrest a little boy named Jamie. He was under arrest for suspicion of murder. Obviously, this chaos that ensued brought the boy and his family to feel terror. We followed Jamie on their way to a police facility. What first struck me was how composed he is, he was just 13, the police just arrested him, and he is made to do things that a child must not experience. I won’t spoil much, but I admire how the legal side of this show was at least ethical. I would have hated it if there’s some legal manipulation happening, but even the arresting officers gave respect to the rights of Jamie and his family too. They showed the video evidence in this episode—it showed Jamie following the victim and ultimately stabbing her—he was, as it stands, guilty. But there’s a feeling of not really. Even without the hints of other possibilities, this video still did not convince me that he did it. Jamie’s father, however, did as many viewers are too. But throughout this show, there is a constant choice between seeing Jamie as pure guilty thus evil and seeing and sympathizing with the idea that he was just another victim in this case or that a mental health problem caused him to do what he did. Nonetheless, basing on the facts, he was guilty right then and there. I personally felt sympathy for him, because I wasn’t convinced yet that he did it for some reason. I also wanted to know the Why before passing any judgement. My brain theorized a scenario that he was just set up or if he in fact did it, there’s some mental health issue at play. I know that sympathizing for a criminal is unethical in all ways, but again, he was still accused and therefore was still innocent to me.

Episode 2: The leads

The police continued finding the Why, they haven’t found the weapon and there is no motive. They went to the school that the victim and Jamie went to. They questioned the school and the students, but were met with various red flags. For one, there was a scene where two boys, which I assume are Jamie’s friends, talking about what happened. They mentioned the knife, which immediately raised a red flag, and a hint that Jamie is not a lone actor. My theory that he was set up came from these two boys. Another red flag was the victim’s best friend. The interview act with her just screams that she knows something or she thinks she knows. Later on, she physically abused one of the boys who is a friend of Jamie—she said that he did it—so once again, a hint that it might not be Jamie alone. That same boy even tried to escape when confronted by the police, he was also arrested after admitting that it was his knife which was used. The police did not question the other boy, which is a bit suspicious to me. Finally, one of the police officer’s sons made some confession which I still don’t fully understand. But that confession made his father think of another angle—Jamie is being bullied. The picture is looking clearer: Jamie, if he did do it, was not alone. There is a possibility of the friends setting him up. I just realized I keep saying “setting him up”, I don’t have a concrete definition to this claim but I mean it in a way that Jamie was either provoked to kill her, his friends changed clothes with him to make it look like it’s him, basically conspiracy stuff. Going back to the point, Jamie was bullied by the victim. I think a quote from the show perfectly summarizes what this particular episode is all about; “What you think is more important than what’s true.” Yes, the video evidence exists, but how do we know if there’s a piece of truth that will explain it even better. I wanted to know the full picture rather than the single evidence that Jamie did it.

Episode 3: A masterpiece, a manipulation, and a man confessing

Episode 3 is one of the most brilliant media I’ve ever watched. It is a masterpiece of storytelling, acting, cinematography—and everything about it feels perfect. The actor that played Jamie really did a very good job.

Manipulation is a central theme to this act. It feels like the psychologist is manipulating Jamie, and Jamie also does the same. It felt like a trick sometimes, but I think the whole act was not a trick but indeed a conversation. If there’s someone tricking, it was Jamie as evident to his multiple outbursts when he said something that might prove him guilty. Jamie’s character is just brilliant for his age, and it was evident by his ability to manipulate what he is saying, it reflected in his ability to hide. The last 20 minutes, which is just a rough estimate, is where all of the dots started connecting. Jamie revealed a part of himself he’s been hiding from us—he finally said things that seemed like a confession. Until now, he’s been firm in his stand that he did not do it. But what we heard from him, that he had a knife that night but he did not touch her… that doing so made him better than other men… is a clear admission of the truth. I felt what the psychologist probably felt—I wanted Jamie to be proven good, I wanted him to be free, I wanted him to continue saying that he did not do it—but that didn’t happen.

Episode 4: Goodbye

Our goodbye with Jamie happened at the end of Episode 3. It will be the last time we will ever see him apart from a call he will make in this last episode.

This episode followed the life of Jamie’s family 13 months after the chaos. What really struck me was how normal their lives seemed until they were reminded by the effects of what Jamie did. The first reminder was the vandalism in their van saying “NONCE,” which is an insult apparently that also means pedophile. This started the anger of the father. As they went to a store to buy paint, another reminder appeared. A man approached the father which he recognizes, the man followed him saying that he sympathized and is on Jamie’s side. The father was reminded of what happened, his mind went blank, but when they were about to leave, he saw the kids who vandalised his car. This made his anger into a long outrage which can be felt throughout the act. His wife and daughter stayed silent in his outburst, when suddenly, they received a call from Jamie.

Jamie wanted to let his father know that he is pleading guilty. Silence was heard, then Jamie’s mother and sister spoke. Jamie was not expecting to have his mother and sister on the call, which hurts to think about because it seems like he did not trust them. The call got cut before his father could say the word “don’t”. Emotions started rising, when they got home, it flooded the house. We got to witness a conversation between the parents about Jamie. This conversation seems like a goodbye, an acknowledgement that they need to move on. The father ended the show with such a powerful scene—he went to his son’s room, cried, then tucked a teddy bear as if putting Jamie to sleep.

I was watching that ending at around 2 AM, I was sobbing, I was writing in my diary, I was devastated. I felt no closure from Jamie, I wanted to see him again even if that means seeing him sentenced to prison. I wanted to know what his future will hold despite all that happened.

Conclusion

To answer the headline—Yes, I did sympathize with the accused killer. I grew to like the facade of this innocent boy who hasn’t been proven guilty yet. But honestly, the truth is clear. Jamie killed the girl without any doubt. I think the reason why I still felt sympathy was because I was seeing the hardship that Jamie went through while the death of the girl just merely echoed in the background. The show followed the life of Jamie, so we only got to see his perspective. I believed in his statements that he did not do it, that he did nothing wrong, because the only voice saying otherwise was that video evidence which I still don’t understand why it was not enough evidence in the first place. The show made me want to know why—to know what Jamie thinks rather than the clear truth in front of me. In the end, I got answers to the whys, but I wanted to know what will happen next. The show ended with minimal closure to what happened to Jamie. It ended without looking back at what happened to the girl. But maybe it’s better that we don’t know. We left Jamie finally admitting to his sin, and we can try and think of what happened to him after that—we can try and feel sorry for him—but it doesn’t change the fact that he was guilty. And the real victims here besides the girl and her family, was Jamie’s family—who suffered the pain of losing a child and suffered the guilt that they allowed all of this to happen.
entry.summary: Here’s a dilemma: An innocent looking, 13-year-old boy, was accused of killing a girl similar to his age. There was concrete video evidence, but there’s a missing piece—more than the weapon, but the Why?

entry.title: Appreciation of creative works
entry.content:
Someone out there is reading a book,
Someone out there is reading a paper,
Someone out there is reading a poem,
Someone out there is watching a film,
Someone out there is watching a show,
Someone out there is watching a video,
Someone out there is listening to music,
Someone out there is listening to a podcast episode,
Someone out there is listening to a speech…

All of them being inspired or touched, feeling joy or sadness, experiencing what it is to be and be in a certain place and time, connecting with characters unknown… Someone out there is forever changed because they saw or heard a work that deeply connected with them.
